claims.text: The initial nanoparticles are single-phase, near-equiatomic, multi-element solid solutions containing elements with significant atomic-size differences.
Atomic-size mismatch introduces severe lattice strain in near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles.
Atomic-size mismatch induces local chemical ordering.
Severe lattice strain creates a kinetic barrier to elemental diffusion.
Strain-induced inhibition of diffusion suppresses phase segregation and chemical de-mixing.
Suppression of diffusion preserves homogeneous structure and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
Annealing approximately 50 K above the upper service temperature enhances atomic mobility.
When thermal energy exceeds the stabilization provided by strain, the diffusion barrier is disrupted.
Disruption of the strain-derived diffusion barrier produces measurable compositional and structural changes.
Catalytic operation typically spans 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use spans 473–1923 K.
Under standard service conditions, the nanoparticles will retain a homogeneous, single-phase structure.
After accelerated annealing, high-strain nanoparticles will show initial phase segregation or local compositional inhomogeneity relative to non-over-annealed nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles receiving no extra annealing will maintain consistent catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Strain-mediated stabilization operates only when atomic-size mismatch is sufficiently large.
Compositions with insufficient atomic-size mismatch may undergo phase separation because the strain-mediated mechanism fails.
Operating substantially beyond the designed thermal window may cause the stabilization mechanism to fail and phase separation to occur.
Choosing elements with large atomic-size differences produces a higher-strain comparison set than choosing elements with similar atomic sizes.
Under identical over-annealing conditions, high-strain nanoparticles should exhibit less phase segregation and compositional deviation than low-strain nanoparticles.
Surface segregation may contribute to observed nanoparticle stability independently of lattice strain.
